          Man Utd Are Better Than Results Suggest, But Michael Carrick’s Side Are Having an Identity Crisis 
        
      
                          
                      Oct 7, 2026
          
                      Ryan Benson / Author, Emily Millen / Design
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
After guiding Manchester United to a third-place finish last season, Michael Carrick has overseen a difficult start to 2026-27. Should he be worried?

When Manchester United appointed Michael Carrick on a permanent two-year deal in the summer, for most it seemed like the only logical choice after he’d taken over halfway through the 2025-26 campaign and steered a side who were unspectacular under Ruben Amorim to a third-place finish. It was a just reward for his impact.
But five matches into the 2026-27 Premier League season and the pressure is on.

After winning 12 of his 17 games in charge last season (all in the Premier League), United have won just two of seven in all competitions this term. Those victories came over promoted Ipswich Town and Champions League debutants Sabah.

A 2-0 defeat at promoted Hull City on the opening day of the season was alarming; United then twice let a lead slip at Everton; they (controversially) lost at home to Manchester City despite having a man advantage for over an hour; they let a two-goal lead slip to a far more vibrant Brighton in the EFL Cup, and they could only draw 1-1 at a Fulham side who began Matchday 5 bottom of the table.
Results have been poor. Performances haven’t been much better.

One particularly notable aspect of United’s games this season is how much more of the ball they’ve generally had. Last term under Carrick, United averaged 49.1% possession; in 2026-27, they’ve had 58% in all competitions and that goes up to 59.9% when just looking at the Premier League, so a 22% increase compared to 2025-26.

We are of course talking about a fairly small sample size in 2026-27, including two games against promoted opposition and having a one-man advantage for so long in the derby, so their possession figure could yet come down. Either way, for now it does feel at odds with the strengths associated with Carrick’s squad – namely the quality they have in transition.
For instance, United impressed in the derby before Phil Foden’s red card, but once the onus was on them to take charge following the sending off, they looked uncomfortable.

Their increased time on the ball will also have some impact on their physical metrics, which have been used as a stick to beat them with in the past few weeks due to them covering less distance per 90 (103.1 kilometres) than all but one Premier League club this term. The discourse has often neglected to mention United’s significantly increased time in possession, though, and that their rankings in some top-line running metrics are pretty similar to last term.

So, the very fact United haven’t covered as much ground as other teams doesn’t mean a great deal in isolation. For example, their 9.9 kilometres covered while sprinting this season is slightly more than City (9.7km) and not massively under Brighton’s (10.6km), and they’ve been two of the best teams in the league in 2026-27.
However, there is arguably a link from this to the idea United have issues with intensity.

Most will look to the midfield pairing here, and understandably so. Among the 57 nominal central/defensive midfielders to play at least 90 minutes in the Premier League this term, Youri Tielemans (4.7) and Kobbie Mainoo (4.0) rank 33rd and 39th respectively for out-of-possession sprints per 90 mins. They’re both excellent footballers, and Mainoo’s start to the season has been quite impressive, though mobility and intensity aren’t aspects you’d associate with either.

United’s collective tally of out-of-possession sprints per 90 (89) is a comparable (in fact, slightly higher) figure to what they averaged under Carrick last season (86), however. When they were winning regularly in 2025-26, you’d have done well to find critics making a big deal about a perceived lack of intensity.

If they do have an issue with intensity, then, it’s probably most pertinent in the context of the team’s structure when pressing, or perhaps even their broader pressing strategy, because there has been a shift from last term.

United have proportionately deployed a high block to a greater extent than any other Premier League team this season (42%) and this is up considerably from Carrick’s time in charge last term (26%). For this to be truly effective, it generally requires a team to deploy a high line; this United side looks uneasy playing in such a way because their defence – not too dissimilar to the midfield – lacks mobility.

Their backline can’t be as high as perhaps it should be, meaning there’s more space for the midfield pairing to occupy between attackers pressing high and defenders dropping deep. It’s not that United are then falling into a low block by default, but if the press is played through, gaps can open up quite quickly and it’s not surprising if the midfielders opt to retreat instead of engage.

As the graphic below highlights, only Aston Villa and Brighton (both 38%) have seen a smaller proportion of their pressures come in the middle third of the pitch than United (39%), who’ve also had the second-smallest share of pressures in their own defensive third (25%).

None of this is inherently bad on its own, of course. It all depends on context, and the introduction of Carlos Baleba – who will be fit for his debut after the international break – should give them more ‘oomph’ in the middle. But there’s a strong argument United might not be best suited to utilising a high block; we’ve noted the lack of mobility further down the pitch, but there’s also questions to be asked about how effective their press is.

As outlined, they’ve spent the greatest proportion of time in a high block among Premier League teams this term, and their 4-2-2-2 out-of-possession shape reflects a fairly aggressive man-to-man press. Or at least that’s presumably the intention.
